questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
1.
  a. Write down any two characteristics of commercial farming (2 Marks)
  b. Write two ways that we can control common diseases of beans (2 Marks)
  c. Differentiate between mono cropping and inter cropping (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Any two: crops/livestock are produced mainly for sale (profit); large-scale farms; high use of capital, machinery, fertilizers and improved seeds; often specialization in one crop or animal (e.g. plantations, ranches); use of hired labour and modern management.
b. Any two: plant certified disease-free seed; practise crop rotation; spray recommended fungicides/pesticides; uproot and burn infected plants (field hygiene); plant resistant varieties; avoid working in the field when plants are wet.
c. Mono cropping is growing a single crop on the same piece of land (often season after season), whereas inter cropping is growing two or more crops together on the same piece of land at the same time (e.g. maize and beans).

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
2.
  a. Distinguish between anthracite and lignite cool (2 Marks)
  b. Write down two significances of energy (2 Marks)
  c. What is meant by energy crises (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Anthracite is the highest-grade, hardest coal with a very high carbon content (about 86–98%), low moisture, burns with a hot, smokeless flame; lignite (brown coal) is the lowest-grade, soft coal with low carbon content (about 25–35%), high moisture, and gives less heat with much smoke.
b. Any two: powers industries and machines; used for transport (fuel for vehicles, ships, aircraft); provides domestic lighting, cooking and heating; generates electricity; earns foreign exchange when exported; creates employment.
c. An energy crisis is a situation where the supply of energy (e.g. oil, electricity) is insufficient to meet demand, usually causing sharp price increases and shortages that disrupt the economy.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
3.
  a. Write down any two advantages of animal and human transport (2 Marks)
  b. Write down any two disadvantages of human and animal transport (2 Marks)
  c. Write any two advantages of rail way transport (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Any two: cheap/affordable; can reach remote areas with no roads; flexible (door-to-door); does not need fuel or expensive infrastructure; causes no pollution.
b. Any two: very slow; carries only small loads; tiring; covers short distances only; animals can be affected by disease, drought and fatigue; unsuitable for perishable goods over long distances.
c. Any two: carries bulky and heavy goods cheaply over long distances; cheaper per tonne-km than road; fewer accidents/safer; less affected by traffic congestion; can carry many passengers at once.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
4.
  a. Explain the two ways in which the temperature effects the agriculture (2 Marks)
  b. Explain the meaning of nitrogen fixing bacteria (2 Marks)
  c. What is the meaning of mixed farming (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Any two: temperature determines the type of crops that can be grown (each crop has an optimum range, e.g. tea in cool highlands, cotton in warm areas); it controls the length of the growing season and rate of crop growth/ripening; very low temperatures (frost) damage crops; high temperatures increase evaporation and water stress.
b. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are soil micro-organisms (e.g. Rhizobium, living in the root nodules of leguminous plants like beans) that convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen compounds (nitrates/ammonia) that plants can use, thereby improving soil fertility.
c. Mixed farming is the growing of crops and the rearing of livestock on the same farm at the same time.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
5.
  a. Explain the main types of the judiciary (2 Marks)
  b. What is the structure of a provincial executive (2 Marks)
  c. What is the national assembly (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Main types/levels of courts: the Supreme (Constitutional) Court – highest court; the Appeal Courts – hear appeals from lower courts; the Regional Courts; and the District (lower/first-instance) Courts. Courts may also be divided into civil and criminal (and military) courts.
b. The provincial (regional) executive is headed by the Regional Governor, assisted by deputy governor(s), district commissioners/mayors and heads of regional departments of the various ministries, who implement government policy in the region.
c. The National Assembly is the national legislature (parliament) made up of elected/appointed representatives; in Somaliland it consists of the House of Representatives and the House of Elders (Guurti). It makes laws, approves the budget and checks the work of the executive.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
6.
  a. Explain the population density (2 Marks)
  b. Differentiate crude population density and agricultural density (2 Marks)
  c. Describe how political factor influence population distribution (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Population density is the average number of people living per unit area of land, usually per square kilometre (Population density = Total population ÷ Total land area).
b. Crude (arithmetic) population density = total population ÷ total land area; agricultural density = number of farmers (rural agricultural population) ÷ area of arable/cultivated land.
c. Any relevant points: political stability and peace attract settlement, while war and insecurity cause people to flee (refugees, displacement); government policies such as resettlement schemes, establishment of capitals/administrative centres, and border or land-use restrictions (e.g. national parks) cause concentration or sparse populations in certain areas.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
7.
  a. Describe any two factors affecting the exploration of minerals (2 Marks)
  b. State the two methods of mining. (2 Marks)
  c. Describe the effects of mining on the environment (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Any two: size/quantity of the deposit; quality (grade) of the ore; mode of occurrence/depth of the deposit; availability of capital and technology; transport and accessibility; market demand and prices; government policy and political stability; availability of labour.
b. Surface mining (e.g. open-cast/open-pit, alluvial, quarrying) and underground mining (e.g. shaft, drift/adit).
c. Any relevant points: destruction of vegetation and land (deforestation, derelict land, open pits); soil erosion; pollution of air, water and soil from dust and chemicals; noise; loss of wildlife habitats; land subsidence.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
8.
  a. Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative maps (2 Marks)
  b. Write any two types relief maps. (2 Marks)
  c. Study the contour map below. Give numbers of the countour lines that are labeled (2 Marks)
     A ____________
     B ____________
     C ____________

diagram.caption: Contour map for Part Two Question 8c: thick index contours labelled 700 (line A, lower left) and 800 (upper right, beside D), with intermediate contour lines; labels B and C mark intermediate contours to be identified.

questions.answer_guide:
a. Quantitative maps show numerical data/amounts (e.g. population density, rainfall totals, using dots, isolines, proportional symbols); qualitative maps show the location or type/kind of features without amounts (e.g. land-use, soil types, vegetation zones).
b. Any two methods of showing relief: contour maps; layer tinting (colour layering); hachures; hill shading; spot heights; trigonometrical stations/bench marks.
c. Interpreted from the map (index contours 700 and 800 with four lines between them = 20 m interval): A = 700 m; B = 740 m; C = 760 m.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
9.
  a. Write down any two characteristics of sub-tropical desert climate (2 Marks)
  b. Write any two functions of soil for plants (2 Marks)
  c. Describe the effects of mining on the environment (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. Any two: very low and unreliable rainfall (below 250 mm per year); very high day temperatures and cold nights (large diurnal range); low humidity and clear skies; high evaporation; strong dry winds and sandstorms.
b. Any two: provides anchorage/support for plant roots; supplies mineral nutrients; stores and supplies water; provides air (oxygen) to roots; habitat for micro-organisms that aid decomposition.
c. (Repeats Question 7c.) Destruction of vegetation and landscape; soil erosion; air, water and soil pollution; noise; loss of wildlife habitats; derelict land and land subsidence.

questions.section: PART TWO: Structured Questions (Answer all the following questions. Each question carries 6 marks)
questions.question:
10. Explain
  a. Elements of environment (3 Marks)
  b. State the process of water cycle. (3 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. The environment is made up of: physical (abiotic) elements – land/relief, water, air/climate, soil, minerals; biological (biotic) elements – plants, animals and micro-organisms; and human (social/cultural) elements – people, settlements, economic and cultural activities.
b. Evaporation – water from oceans, lakes and rivers is heated by the sun and turns into water vapour (with transpiration from plants); Condensation – the vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds; Precipitation – water falls back to earth as rain, snow or hail; Run-off/Infiltration (collection) – water flows over the surface into rivers and seas or seeps into the ground, and the cycle repeats.
